title: Act I, Scene III

teacherSummary.text: On the heath the Witches hail Macbeth as Thane of Glamis, Thane of Cawdor and 'king hereafter', and tell Banquo he will 'get kings, though thou be none.' They vanish. Ross and Angus arrive to tell Macbeth he is now Thane of Cawdor. Macbeth, startled, imagines murder ('horrible imaginings') and decides 'chance may crown me'; Banquo warns that 'instruments of darkness tell us truths' to betray us.

context.history: Prophecy was a dangerous subject: predicting a monarch's death could be treason. Banquo's line about 'instruments of darkness' reflects the period's belief that the devil tells half-truths to trap souls.

significance: The scene splits two responses to the same temptation: Banquo is wary, Macbeth is already thinking of murder. Whether the prophecy causes the crime or reveals a desire already there is the play's central question about fate and free will.
discussionQuestions: If a fortune teller's first prediction came true, would you trust the second? Why or why not?
Where does foreshadowing appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with appearance versus reality?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act I, Scene III,” how does Shakespeare show the prophecies and their pull? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act I, Scene III, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of the prophecies and their pull? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the foreshadowing in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act I, Scene III develops the idea of the prophecies and their pull. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of foreshadowing and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act I, Scene III (where it begins, turns and ends) and its foreshadowing shape the reader's understanding of the prophecies and their pull. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act I, Scene III suggests about the prophecies and their pull. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's foreshadowing and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses foreshadowing in Act I, Scene III to complicate the reader's understanding of the prophecies and their pull. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act I, Scene III within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of the prophecies and their pull responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act I, Scene III alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of the prophecies and their pull follows or bends those conventions, using the foreshadowing as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act I, Scene III and its treatment of the prophecies and their pull. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's foreshadowing and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act I, Scene III as evidence for a larger claim about the prophecies and their pull in Macbeth. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act I, Scene III as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of the prophecies and their pull. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Macbeth.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: If a fortune teller's first prediction came true, would you trust the second? Why or why not? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script:
Today's words are shipman, enkindle, treasons, soliciting, selfsame. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “I myself have all the other,
And the very ports they blow,
All the quarters that they know
I’ the shipman’s card.” In this sentence it means: a sailor. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Macbeth would have known. Prophecy was a dangerous subject: predicting a monarch's death could be treason. Banquo's line about 'instruments of darkness' reflects the period's belief that the devil tells half-truths to trap souls. Why does this scene matter? The scene splits two responses to the same temptation: Banquo is wary, Macbeth is already thinking of murder. Whether the prophecy causes the crime or reveals a desire already there is the play's central question about fate and free will. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for foreshadowing.
segments.script:
Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “A sailor’s wife had chestnuts in her lap,
And munch’d, and munch’d, and munch’d:—“Give me,”” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to the prophecies and their pull? I circle “chestnuts”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find foreshadowing, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for foreshadowing.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of foreshadowing. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how Act I, Scene III develops the idea of the prophecies and their pull. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of foreshadowing and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this scene connect to ambition and its costs? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Scene quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the scene quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this scene suggests about the prophecies and their pull, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how foreshadowing shapes the prophecies and their pull. Tonight, read the next scene and add two words to your etymology log.

provenance: Original Liber et Libri pilot content; modern contextual vocabulary definitions (curated, based on Princeton WordNet 3.0); word histories only where verified (Online Etymology Dictionary); quotations from the public-domain text.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
